newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Afghanistan calls on Taleban to pull out of Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Afghanistan calls on Taleban to pull out of Kabul.

text.p: Afghan deputy Foreign Minister Abdul Rahim Ghafoorzai called on the Islamic Taleban movement on Wednesday to evacuate Kabul, which it captured three weeks ago, and for an international police force to ensure the city's security.

Negotiations should then begin on forming an interim government of national unity, he told the Security Council at the start of a debate requested by Russia and several Central Asian republics concerned by the upsurge of fighting near their southern borders.
If these proposals were not accepted, the Afghan armed forces would "resort to action to end this catastrophic situation" in Kabul, Ghafoorzai said.
While the government had the ability "to enter and liberate" the city, it was withholding action to avoid civilian casualties and further destruction.
Some 30 speakers took part in the debate, which was adjourned without a date being set for its continuation.

No resolution was formally submitted but almost all speakers called for a halt to the fighting, negotiations to form a broad-based government and an end to outside interference. A number also criticised the treatment of women and other reported human rights violations by Taleban.
Ghafoorza said an immediate ceasefire would be observed if "the Taleban armed forces...evacuate the capital immediately" and withdrew their heavy weapons beyond artillery range.
Kabul must be recognised as a demilitarized zone and a police force formed under the supervision of the United Nations and the Organisation of the Islamic Conference to ensure its security, he said.

"Negotiations should start to pave the way for the formation of an interim government of national unity in the capital city of Kabul," said Ghafoorzai, who devoted much of his speech to accusing Pakistan of sponsoring Taleban and blaming U.N. officials for turning a blind eye.

Ghafoorzai repeated previous calls for the United Nations to send a fact-finding mission to Afghanistan, saying it should also look into what he alleged was the use of chemical weapons against government troops in battles east of Kabul.

Russian U.N. envoy Sergei Lavrov said Russia considered "the approach of the flames of war in neighbouring Afghanistan toward the borders of the Commonwealth (of Independent States)" as a direct threat to its national interests and security and to stability in the region.
Russia had repeatedly "drawn attention to fact that the Security Council must be more active in dealing with the problems of Afghanistan and not consign these problems to oblivion," he said.

Pakistan's Minister of State for Foreign Affairs, Sahibzada Muhammad Nazeer Sultan, said his country had "no favourites in Afghanistan" and believed only an intra-Afghan political process leading to a broad-based government would allow the return of a durable peace.

He proposed a resolution calling for an immediate cessation of hostilities; affirming the unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity of Afghanistan; calling on all states to respect the principle of non-intervention; and imposing an immediate arms embargo on Afghanistan, with monitoring of both the ceasefire and embargo.
American U.N. envoy Madeleine Albright called on all parties to stop fighting and begin negotiations for a political settlement.

"There can be no lasting military solution to this conflict. There can be no durable peace in Afghanistan until a broad-based government is formed which represents and respects the rights of all of Afghanistan's diverse peoples," she said.
